title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment (N=300 matched intents: 150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants) to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate generation contract we executed one shared LLM generation per paired intent, validated the same candidate with two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and allowed up to one repair call only if a validator reported forbidden reachability. The run completed planned 600 episodes (300 pairs), used model_calls_used = 300, and produced a degenerate confirmatory outcome: baseline_success_count = 300, guarded_success_count = 300 (paired contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). No validator ever reported forbidden reachability, no repair was invoked, McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0, and the prespecified paired-bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Because the repair path was never exercised, these results quantify that, under the exact protocol and artifacts used here, inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the safety predicate; the experiment provides no evidence about verifier-guided repair ability to rescue genuine violations. We archive the preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, per-episode validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to inform follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency but raises well-known safety concerns: generated configurations can expand attack surface or violate access-control constraints. Prior system and survey work therefore recommend constrained generation, execution oracles, or generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as risk mitigations. Yet confirmation that a verifier placed inside a GVR loop meaningfully reduces security-relevant (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations under adversarial inputs remains scarce. We address the focused operational question: does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? We conducted a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic emulation and validators to obtain an auditable confirmatory answer under a fixed contract.
sections.related_work: Three streams motivated our design. First, GVR and execution-guided repair systems for code and infrastructure have shown that verifier feedback can improve correctness, but realized gains depend strongly on verifier power and repair strategy. Second, NetOps and LLM surveys document LLM failure modes—hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch—and consistently recommend validators or human oversight to reduce operational risk. Third, emulation/testbed research demonstrates that execution-based validation is feasible for controlled evaluation but highlights external-validity gaps when moving to production hardware or live traffic. Existing literature rarely combines preregistration, deterministic paired designs, and archived per-episode verifier traces tailored to security reachability predicates; our study occupies that methodological niche and provides an artifact-backed case study of the consequences of specific generation semantics and verifier choices.
sections.methodology:
Design and estimand: We preregistered a paired binary design (N=300 matched intents: 150 benign seeds + 150 programmatic adversarial variants) with primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportions yielding forbidden reachability). The confirmatory test was an exact McNemar two-sided test (α=0.05); confidence intervals were to be computed by bootstrap percentile.

Generation semantics and adapter contract: To conserve model-call budget under a hosted-provider contract we used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each pair a single LLM candidate was generated and replayed to both arms (baseline and guarded). This produces model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs instead of 600 independent draws. This contract reduces between-arm sampling variance and the probability of discordant pairs (which are necessary to evaluate repair efficacy) and is therefore a central design choice that affects sensitivity to repair.

Intervention and repair policy: Baseline = replay of the shared initial candidate. Guarded = the same shared candidate validated by two deterministic validators; if any validator reported forbidden reachability, up to one repair LLM call was allowed (maximum one repair per pair). Repair attempts were only triggered by validator-detected forbidden reachability.

Validators, scoring, and determinism: The preregistration specified two deterministic validators: a containerized execution-style reachability validator (preregistered as Batfish in the evidence bundle) and a lightweight graph-based static reachability analyzer. We combined their binary judgments with a logical-OR decision rule: a pair was labeled violating if any validator reported forbidden reachability. All orchestration and sampler seeds were fixed and the emulation environment was Dockerized to ensure deterministic replay; per-episode validator traces and scoring decisions were archived.

Power, planned analysis, and minor deviation: The preregistered power plan targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction with N=300 and prespecified 1,000 bootstrap resamples for CI estimation. During final analysis we increased bootstrap resamples to 10,000 (bootstrap_seed = 1729) to reduce Monte Carlo error; this deviation is recorded in the archived analysis log and disclosed in the mandatory Disclosure Statement.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions) with completed = 600 and failed = 0; model_calls_used = 300 under the shared_initial_candidate contract.

Primary confirmatory outcome: All 300 matched pairs satisfied the forbidden-reachability safety predicate in both arms: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300. The paired contingency is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. The prespecified paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.0, 0.0].

Degenerate contingency and descriptive bound: The absence of discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0) renders the McNemar test uninformative about repair efficacy because there are no candidate disagreements to repair. This degenerate outcome stems from two coupled factors in our design: (1) the shared_initial_candidate semantics reduced independent-sample variability between arms, and (2) none of the adversarial variants produced a validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the chosen model and validators. As a descriptive constraint, observing 0 violations in 300 independent episodes gives a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the baseline violation probability of 1 − 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%).

Repair and validator traces: Validators never reported forbidden reachability for any initial candidate; consequently no repair calls were invoked and all per-episode repair_applied flags are false. Validator judgments were concordant across the deterministic validators for every archived episode. Representative per-episode traces (validation_before/after, final_configuration, difficulty annotations) are archived and show consistent validity markings and zero violation codes.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: Under the exact preregistered contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt-5-mini), evaluated deterministic validator set combined by logical OR, emulator, and the programmatic adversarial perturbations used here, baseline generation produced no validator-detectable forbidden reachability across the sampled intents; therefore inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. The archived artifacts allow independent verification of provider-call accounting, per-episode validator traces, and the degenerate paired contingency.

What we do not show: Because the repair path was never exercised, this experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction; the observed degenerate contingency violates that assumption and renders the confirmatory McNemar inference moot regarding repair efficacy. The null paired difference should therefore not be interpreted as general evidence that verifiers are unnecessary.

Design lessons and operational implications: (1) Generation semantics matter: shared_initial_candidate reduces hosted-model cost but suppresses independent draws that could produce discordant failures the repair step might correct. For experiments or deployments intended to exercise repair efficacy, independent-condition generation (two independent LLM draws per pair) or increased repair-call budgets are preferable. (2) Adversary potency matters: the deterministic adversarial perturbations used here did not trigger validator-detectable violations for the evaluated model and validators; stronger, targeted adversaries against the verifier predicates are required for stress tests that probe repair. (3) Verifier strength and diversity matter: we evaluated two deterministic validators combined by logical OR; production deployments or stress tests should consider broader oracle diversity and higher-fidelity execution oracles. (4) Deterministic reproducible accounting is practicable: fixed seeds, containerized emulation, and archived per-episode validator traces enable exact audit of outcomes and provider-call budget trade-offs.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is limited by shared_initial_candidate semantics and the single-model scope. Construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two validators adequately capture operational security risk. External validity is constrained by synthetic tasks and deterministic FRRouting-style emulation; real production heterogeneity and live traffic may reveal different failure modes. Conclusion validity is limited because the observed contingency is degenerate and preregistered power assumptions are unmet. These limitations motivate targeted follow-up tests rather than reinterpretation of the present confirmatory result.
sections.conclusion: We ran a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation (declared model gpt-5-mini) with two deterministic validators combined by logical OR and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract. The run completed N=300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair path was not exercised and the experiment cannot speak to verifier-guided repair efficacy. The results highlight that generation semantics (shared vs independent draws), adversary design, repair budget, verifier strength, and model diversity materially determine whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations. We release the preregistration and deterministic artifacts to inform and enable reproducible follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise repair paths.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in the evidence bundle for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in deterministic FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
